text: Before sunrise on the 14th of September 1951, 14 fishing boats were working a reef off the
Cape Coast of South Africa when their skippers saw a man wading through the sea.
He was 30 feet tall.
The water on that reef is 21 feet deep at low tide and it came up to his chest.
By the end of that morning every boat in the fleet had turned for home and not one
of them went back out to that reef again, not in 50 years of trying.
The skipper wrote it all down in his logbook in his own hand and then he wrote down why.
That book sat in a sea chest for 70 years.

Huck by South Africa 1951.
A fishing village of about 300 people, 30 miles of wind scoured coast from the nearest
town with one harbor wall, one chapel and a smokehouse that stank so badly the dogs
would not go near it.
The reef that fed the village lay 400 yards off the point.
The old fisherman called it the scary.
A long low spine of black rock that broke the surface at low water and hid itself at high
and it held more snook and cabel juke than anywhere on that stretch of coast.
Every boat in Huck by worked it at first light and in 30 years nobody had ever lost
a man there because they all knew the scary the way you know the inside of your
own mouth.
Four people left records of what happened there on that September morning and not
one of them ever compared notes.
The first was the skipper of the lead boat Peter Visser, 52 years old, a broad
sunburned man with a missing finger and a habit of writing his log book in pencil
on the back of a seed calendar.
He had fished the scary since he was 12 and in all that time according to his
wife he had never once written a line he could not swear to before a
magistrate.
The second was the harbour master Rudolf Brink, a heavy, careful man who recorded
every boat in and out in a ledger as long as a coffin and who on the day in
question wrote down something he had never recorded before.
The third was the keeper of the lighthouse on the point, a widow named
Anitji Kloiti who kept a night log of every light, every squall, every
dawn is a single shaky line and the force was a young fisheries officer from
the city, a 26 year old with spectacles and a government notebook who had
come out to the Cape that week to count fish and who by an accident of
timing that he would regret for the rest of his life was standing on the
key when the boats came home start with the skipper's lock.
It is a small soft grease stained book bound in oil cloth and the entry for
the 14th begins the way every entry begins.
14 boats cast off 430 all to the scary.
Then in the same steady pencil a line that comes a little after the others.
Light gray in the east sea flat hauling first lines 5.41 dead calm of a
kind I have not seen on this coast.
Birds went quiet.
Every man stopped working.
What he does not say and what he told his wife that night is that the
sound went out of the world.
The engines were running but he could not hear them.
The gulls had been wheeling in their hundreds over the boats and
they all dropped onto the water at once and sat there silent.
The way birds sit before a storm.
Then Peter Visser looked up because the youngest man on his crew a boy of 17
named Danny Pretorius had taken hold of his sleeve and was pointing north.
400 yards beyond the bow of the sea Martin in the gray light.
Something was moving through the water along the line of the reef.
The skippers first thought which he wrote down honestly was that a
whale had come in.
His second thought was that whales do not walk.
The third a moment later was a sentence he put in the log in letters so
large that they run off the edge of the page.
It is a man.
He was walking along the scary in water that on the chart read 21
feet at low tide and the water came up to his chest.
He was moving slowly and the sea parted in front of him in a long
smooth swell that rolled out toward the boats and lifted them
one by one as it passed.
His shoulders and head were above the surface dark and wet in the
gray light and the skipper who had spent 40 years judging distance on
that water wrote that he reckoned him at 30 feet from crown to heel
because he could see the line of the water on his ribs and knew
the depth he was standing in.
He did not hurry.
Every few steps he stopped bent from the waist and laid his
open hand flat against the bottom the way a man puts his palm on a
sleeping animal to feel it breathe.
Then he straightened took another step and did it again at 549
by the skipper's watch.
He stopped in the middle of the reef a long stone's throw from
the sea marting and slowly toned his head.
He looked at the boats and Peter Vissa who wrote the next line
with a pencil that had gone dull and pressed through the
page said that he knew in that moment he was not being looked
at as the thing looks at prey.
He was being looked at the way a man looks at a stranger who
has parked a cart across his gate.
